grammar.title: Grammatik
grammar.rule: Ich mache den Schrank auf. · Ich kann den Schrank aufmachen.
grammar.note_en:
Some verbs contain a stressed first part which separates in an ordinary present-tense main clause. Aufmachen means “open”: Ich mache den Schrank auf (“I open the cupboard”). The finite verb takes the familiar verb position; auf stands at the end. Zumachen means “close”: Mira macht den Umschlag zu (“Mira closes the envelope”). The meanings build on öffnen and the state offen/zu, but learn each whole verb as a vocabulary item. Not every prefix can be combined freely with every verb.

The same bracket appears with einkaufen (“shop/buy provisions”), mitbringen (“bring along”), aufräumen (“tidy/clear away”), aufstehen (“stand/get up”), anrufen (“call by phone”), anfangen (“begin”) and aufhören (“stop”). Nora kauft Milch ein is buying provisions; Nora bringt Milch mit adds bringing them back to the group. Clearing a table makes space by moving objects; putzen removes dirt. Ben hears Mira (Ben hört Mira) but stops his work (Ben hört auf). The particle changes the meaning: aufhören is not simply another occurrence of hören. Anfangen has the stem change shown in the story: wir fangen an, Ben fängt an. Do not extend that changed stem to wir.

The main-clause verb position still follows chapter8. With a fronted time or place, the finite verb precedes the subject: Heute ruft Emil Ada an (“Today Emil calls Ada”). With a modal, the entire infinitive stays together at the end: Ich kann den Schrank aufmachen (“I can open the cupboard”), Ich kann Ada anrufen (“I can phone Ada”). Do not separate auf machen or an rufen in these infinitives. The finite verb in those sentences is kann. The table shows only forms read in the story; it is not a complete paradigm.

These separable prefixes carry lexical stress: AUFmachen, ZUmachen, AUFräumen, MITbringen, ANrufen, EINkaufen, AUFstehen, ANfangen and AUFhören. Capitals here are an English-note stress display, not German spelling; actual German verbs remain lower-case unless starting a sentence. Hören (“hear/listen”), spielen (“play”), passen (“fit”), schicken (“send”), besuchen (“visit”) and versuchen (“try”) do not split in the main clauses here. The unstressed beginnings be- in besuchen and ver- in versuchen stay attached. Learn these contrasts with their words, not as a claim that every German verb ending in -en behaves the same way. There is no audio requirement.

Versuchen can take a noun object: einen Weg ohne Schlüssel versuchen (“try a method without a key”). This uses known noun-case grammar and does not teach an infinitive with zu. The story separately says Wir versuchen einen Weg ohne Schlüssel (“We try a way without a key”) and Wir kaufen heute keinen Schrank (“We are not buying a cupboard today”). Anfangen similarly takes die Arbeit, or stands by itself before a separate sentence describing reading. Aufhören stands by itself when Ben puts his hammer down. Do not join these clauses with an untaught infinitive construction. The noun-object construction for versuchen is documented by the IDS German verb-valency dictionary: https://grammis.ids-mannheim.de/verbs/view/401093/1 .

Schrank is a cupboard, Umschlag an envelope, Einladung an invitation. The old note asks Ada to come on a Saturday at nine. No year identifies that Saturday; the group’s present reading hour begins at ten. The envelope has no postal address, the old note remains in the house and Ada does not know it. Emil chooses a call rather than sending this note. The text does not solve why the old invitation stayed here, supply a year for the photograph, or identify who removed the notebook page. Ada is heard remotely; her visit is still ahead.

Vorsichtig means “carefully”, with care to avoid damage; langsam means “slowly”. Plötzlich marks the unexpected discovery or change of focus (“suddenly”), while endlich marks the welcome arrival of a result after waiting (“at last”). A careful action need not always be slow, and a sudden discovery need not be an achieved goal: these are separate meanings. The delivered references and nearby state contrasts precede the drills. English meanings in the closed banks identify the intended sense; the answer still requires the appropriate German word. Arrow items require the finite verb and subject together, retaining the separated particle at the end.

Reference-table translations: Ich mache den Schrank nicht auf — “I do not open the cupboard”; Du kaufst Milch ein — “You buy milk”; Nora bringt Milch mit — “Nora brings milk along”; Emil ruft Ada an — “Emil phones Ada”. Wir fangen die Arbeit an — “We begin the work”; Ben fängt die Arbeit an — “Ben begins the work”; Wir hören auf — “We stop”; Ben hört auf — “Ben stops”. Ich kann den Schrank aufmachen — “I can open the cupboard”; Mira kann die Kiste zumachen — “Mira can close the box”; Ich kann Brot mitbringen — “I can bring bread along”; Ich kann Ada anrufen — “I can phone Ada”. The shorter contrasts wir fangen an and Ben fängt an mean “we begin” and “Ben begins”; Ben hört Mira means “Ben hears Mira”. Nora kauft Milch ein means “Nora buys milk”; Nora bringt Milch mit means “Nora brings milk along”.

A.instruction: For arrow items, use two words: the finite verb followed by the same subject word as in the source sentence. Keep the final particle.

B.title: B — Wörter
B.instruction: Use the English meanings in order. First bank: cupboard; envelope; letter; key (example: chair). Second bank: carefully; slowly; suddenly; at last (example: at last). Some words may repeat. Keep each word as printed.

items.prompt: Kann Ben den ___ öffnen?
Mira trägt den ___ nicht auf die Straße.
Liegt der ___ im Umschlag?
Passt der ___ nicht?
Mira macht den Umschlag ___ auf.
Wir arbeiten heute ___.
Nora sieht ___ den Umschlag.
Ist der Schrank ___ offen?
Der Schlüssel passt nicht. Was versuchen die Leute?
model_answers: Sie versuchen einen Weg ohne Schlüssel.
Ben will den Schrank ohne Schlüssel aufmachen.
items.rubric: Name the alternative to the failed entrance key, not a newly found cupboard key.

items.prompt: Was räumt Mira auf?
model_answers: Mira bringt das Heft an das Fenster.
items.rubric: Clearing is moving the notebook to the window table, not wiping dirt.

items.prompt: Was liegt jetzt auf dem Tisch an der Wand?
model_answers: Eine Tür liegt auf dem Tisch.
Auf dem Tisch liegt die Tür.
items.rubric: One cupboard door has been removed. The notebook has moved to the window table.

items.prompt: Was kauft Nora ein und bringt Nora mit?
items.rubric: Milk is the provision Nora buys and brings back; the child accompanies her rather than being a purchase.

items.prompt: Was ist im Umschlag?
items.rubric: Accept the paper as a letter and its function as an invitation. It is distinct from the notebook’s missing page.

items.prompt: Schickt Emil die Einladung? Was macht Emil?
model_answers: Er schickt die Einladung nicht. Er ruft Ada an.
items.rubric: He chooses the phone call; do not claim that he visits Ada or sends this old invitation.

items.prompt: Was will Ada heute machen?
items.rubric: Accept reading, seeing the people, coming to/visiting the house; she is on the phone and has not arrived.

items.prompt: Was willst du heute anfangen?
model_answers: Ich will heute die Arbeit anfangen.
Ich will heute das Buch lesen.
items.rubric: Personal answer: accept any licensed coherent intention. For anfangen, a direct activity noun or separate sentence is enough; no untaught zu-infinitive.
